audit.method: Each maintained diagnostic pathway is separated into challenge, observable symptoms, methodological response, and targeted improvement. Symptom matching is qualitative differential diagnosis for hypothesis generation; it is not a probability, confidence score, or automatic prescription.
audit.evidence_policy: Evidence coverage describes documentation scope only. Exact component support means that at least one displayed pathway reference directly addresses the selected component; pathway-level synthesis means the displayed evidence supports the broader pathway but is not claimed as exact support for every subclaim in the component.
audit.verification_policy: Interventions are retained only after pathway-specific checks improve relevant Design–Performance outcomes. Lack of improvement triggers re-diagnosis rather than automatic escalation to a stronger method.

checks: Compare error or residual energy across low- and high-frequency bands instead of relying only on a global norm.
Track learning curves by spatial or temporal frequency to test whether fine scales are learned systematically later.
Compare local error in oscillatory regions against smoother regions under the same training budget.
confirmation_metrics: Local relative error in oscillatory regions
tradeoffs: Richer Fourier, sinusoidal, or multiscale representations can improve high-frequency resolution while increasing parameter, evaluation, or tuning cost.
Frequency curricula may improve trainability but add scheduling choices and extra training stages.

checks: Inspect local error and oscillation immediately upstream and downstream of shocks, interfaces, or sharp fronts.
Check conservation, entropy, or other admissibility diagnostics rather than accepting a low global residual alone.
Compare strong-form and weak / conservative residual behavior near the discontinuity.
tradeoffs: Weak, variational, or conservative formulations can improve admissibility while adding quadrature, interface, or local-balance cost.
Interface-aware decomposition can localize sharp features but introduces transmission and continuity conditions that must also be verified.

metrics: cost of quadrature or interface enforcement

checks: Evaluate BC, IC, and interface violations separately from the interior PDE residual.
Plot spatially localized boundary or interface error and compare it with nearby interior error.
Repeat training across penalty weights to determine whether constraint satisfaction is weight-sensitive.
tradeoffs: Hard constraints can improve exact satisfaction but may complicate the trial space, geometry handling, or conditioning.
Augmented-Lagrangian or constrained formulations can reduce penalty sensitivity while adding auxiliary variables or update overhead.

checks: Compute integral mass, momentum, energy, or other conserved-quantity balance independently of pointwise field error.
Measure flux mismatch across interfaces, control-volume faces, or subdomain boundaries.
Inspect local balance residuals to identify regions where global cancellation hides conservation error.
tradeoffs: Conservative or control-volume residuals can improve physical fidelity while adding quadrature, stencil, or interface-evaluation cost.
Stronger local balance enforcement can reshape loss conditioning and may require dedicated scaling or balancing.

checks: Profile derivative evaluation separately from the rest of the training step to identify graph-depth and memory bottlenecks.
Track memory, wall-clock time, and failure rate as derivative order or spatial dimension increases.
Compare residual consistency between automatic differentiation and an independent discrete or analytical operator check.
tradeoffs: First-order or mixed reformulations reduce AD depth but add auxiliary variables and compatibility constraints.
Numerical or discrete differentiation may reduce graph cost while introducing discretization choices that require independent consistency checks.

metrics: operator / residual consistency and field error

checks: Plot each objective term and its gradient norm rather than only the summed loss.
Measure gradient alignment or conflict between PDE, boundary, initial-condition, and data objectives.
Repeat training under modest changes in loss weights to test whether convergence is dominated by manual weighting.
tradeoffs: Adaptive balancing can improve trainability while requiring extra gradient statistics, kernel information, or constrained updates.
Aggressively equalizing objective magnitudes does not guarantee that every objective has equal scientific importance.

metrics: BC / IC and PDE errors separately

checks: Evaluate error or residual on an independent held-out point set that is not reused for training.
Plot spatial or temporal coverage together with held-out error to identify missed layers, interfaces, or sparse regions.
Compare candidate resampling policies at a matched total residual-evaluation budget.
confirmation_metrics: Coverage of boundary layers and interfaces
Accuracy per collocation-point or residual-call budget
tradeoffs: Adaptive sampling can reduce localized error while adding search, resampling, or residual-evaluation cost.
Concentrating points in high-residual regions can reduce coverage elsewhere, so independent validation points remain necessary.

metrics: point count / residual-call cost and seed sensitivity

checks: Map error by subregion, material, or scale to test whether failure is localized rather than global.
Measure interface continuity and flux errors when comparing monolithic and decomposed formulations.
Profile strong / weak scaling, communication, and synchronization overhead when parallel execution is claimed.
tradeoffs: Domain decomposition can improve localization and parallel scaling while introducing interface constraints and multi-network coordination.
Parallel execution can reduce wall time without reducing total computational work and may add communication overhead.

checks: Plot field error and phase error as functions of time rather than only at the final or aggregate level.
Compare early- and late-time residuals to test for causal imbalance or temporal forgetting.
Repeat with progressively longer horizons to identify the interval at which stability degrades.
tradeoffs: Time marching or temporal decomposition can stabilize long horizons while introducing sequential dependence, window interfaces, or retraining overhead.
Causal curricula may improve optimization but require schedule and horizon choices that remain problem dependent.

checks: Inspect total and per-objective gradient norms together with optimizer step acceptance or line-search behavior.
Compare convergence across several random initializations before attributing a plateau to the architecture alone.
Evaluate the effect of non-dimensionalization or variable scaling before escalating optimizer complexity.
confirmation_metrics: Iterations and wall-clock to target error
tradeoffs: Second-order or quasi-Newton steps can reduce iteration count while increasing memory or per-step cost.
Staged optimizers and continuation can improve basin access while adding additional training phases and hyperparameters.

checks: Compare state error and parameter error separately; a good state fit does not establish correct parameter recovery.
Inspect parameter correlations or sensitivity to perturbations in observations to test practical identifiability.
Repeat inference under controlled noise and alternative observation layouts to test whether the recovered parameters are observation-dependent.
tradeoffs: Additional observations or stronger priors can improve identifiability while increasing data-acquisition requirements or prior dependence.
Bayesian inference can expose non-identifiability but substantially increases computational and convergence demands.

checks: Separate offline training cost from online inference cost and report the break-even point for repeated use.
Evaluate accuracy across held-out parameter sets rather than only configurations seen during training.
Measure transfer or operator-model degradation under extrapolation beyond the training parameter distribution.
tradeoffs: Operator or meta-learning can sharply reduce online cost while requiring larger offline training sets and broader parameter-space coverage.
Amortized models may lose accuracy outside the training distribution, so reuse claims require held-out and extrapolation checks.

checks: Evaluate interval or posterior coverage against held-out observations or known synthetic truth rather than inspecting uncertainty width alone.
Separate data / parameter uncertainty from approximation uncertainty where the method claims to distinguish them.
Test calibration under increasing noise and distribution shift instead of reporting only in-distribution point accuracy.
tradeoffs: Bayesian, ensemble, or variational methods can improve uncertainty characterization while multiplying training, sampling, or inference cost.
Wider intervals can improve nominal coverage without improving decision usefulness; calibration and sharpness must be interpreted together.
